title: Water into Wine and the Cleansing of the Temple
summary: At a wedding in Cana, when the wine runs out, Jesus has servants fill six stone purification jars with water, which becomes the best wine of the feast. John calls this the first of his signs, revealing his glory. At Passover in Jerusalem, Jesus drives the animal sellers and money changers out of the temple courts and, when challenged for a sign, speaks of destroying this temple and raising it in three days, meaning his body.
story: Chapter 1 ended with Jesus promising Nathanael that he would see greater things. Here the first of them happens, on the third day after the calling of Philip and Nathanael. The two scenes of this chapter belong together. In Cana, Jesus replaces the water of Jewish purification with abundant wine; in Jerusalem, he confronts the temple and speaks of his own body as the true temple. Both show that something new has arrived that fulfills and surpasses Israel's institutions. The chapter also introduces two threads that run through the Gospel: Jesus' hour, which has not yet come, and the pattern of signs that some believe and others misunderstand. The disciples' faith appears at Cana and deepens only after the resurrection.
historical:
Cana was a village in Galilee, mentioned only in John; its site is debated, with Khirbet Qana, north of Nazareth, favored by many archaeologists, and the traditional site at Kafr Kanna, near Nazareth, favored by pilgrims. Capernaum, on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, served as Jesus' base. Archaeologists have found many stone vessels from first-century Judea and Galilee, and Jewish purity law held that stone, unlike pottery, did not become ritually unclean. The six large jars reflect a household concerned with purity.

The temple Jesus entered was Herod the Great's, begun around 20 or 19 BC. The leaders' remark that it had taken forty-six years to build places this Passover around AD 27 or 28, a useful clue for dating Jesus' ministry, though the building work itself continued until the 60s. Matthew, Mark, and Luke place the temple cleansing in Jesus' last week, while John places it at the beginning. Some scholars think there were two cleansings, one early and one late. Others think there was one, and that John placed it at the start for theological reasons, or that the Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, and Luke, so called because they see the story with a common eye), which record only one Jerusalem visit, placed it at the end because that was their only setting.
cultural:
A village wedding could last several days, and the bridegroom's family was expected to provide food and wine for the guests. Running out of wine would bring public shame on the family in a culture where honor and hospitality mattered greatly. Jesus' address to his mother as Woman sounds cold in English, but it was a respectful form of address (he uses it on the cross in 19:26 as he entrusts her to the beloved disciple), though it does mark a distance: his actions are governed by his hour, not by family request. The master of the banquet was the guest or servant in charge of the feast.

In the temple's outer court, sellers provided animals for sacrifice, which pilgrims who traveled long distances could not easily bring with them, and money changers exchanged the coinage of the Roman world for the Tyrian silver coins required for the annual temple tax. The trade was legal and practical. Jesus' objection, in John's wording, is that his Father's house had become a marketplace, which recalls Zechariah 14:21, where in the day of the Lord there will no longer be a merchant in the house of the Lord.
literary: John tells the Cana story with great economy, and much is left unsaid: we never learn how the water became wine, only that the servants knew. The story's key sentence is its conclusion in verse 11, which labels it the first of His signs and says it revealed His glory. The temple scene follows John's characteristic pattern of misunderstanding: Jesus speaks of a temple, his hearers think of the building, and the narrator explains that he meant his body. The disciples understand only later, after the resurrection, and John openly tells the reader that their memory and faith were shaped by what came after (verse 22). The closing verses (23 to 25) form a bridge to Nicodemus in chapter 3: many believed because of signs, but Jesus did not entrust himself to them, because he knew what was in a man.

outline.t: A wedding at Cana; the wine runs out
The first sign reveals his glory
Destroy this temple: the sign of his body
Faith based on signs; Jesus knows the heart

doctrines.note: The prophets pictured the messianic age as a time of abundant wine (Amos 9:13, Joel 3:18). By providing more than a hundred gallons of the best wine, Jesus signals that the age of promise has arrived. His glory is revealed, and his disciples believe.

Jesus' zeal for his Father's house shows that God's presence and worship are holy and must not be turned into commerce. Yet he also points beyond the building to his own body as the place where God is present.

Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up: Jesus predicts his own resurrection and claims to be its agent. The disciples' faith after the resurrection rested on Scripture and on Jesus' own word fulfilled.

words.note: Sēmeion, sign. John's preferred word for Jesus' miracles, chosen because they point beyond themselves to who he is. The other Gospels more often use a word meaning mighty works. In John, signs can lead to faith (verse 11) but can also produce a shallow belief that Jesus does not trust (verses 23 to 25).

Hōra, hour. My hour has not yet come. Throughout John, Jesus' hour refers to the time of his death, resurrection, and return to the Father (12:23, 13:1, 17:1). Even at a wedding, his actions are ordered toward that hour.

Naos, temple, specifically the sanctuary where God dwelt, as distinct from the whole temple complex (hieron) where the traders were. Jesus uses naos for his body. John has already said the Word tabernacled among us (1:14); now Jesus is the true dwelling place of God.

christ: Both scenes reveal Jesus as the one in whom Israel's hopes are fulfilled. At Cana he provides the wine of the promised age, and he does it by transforming water set apart for purification, a sign that he brings what the old rites pointed toward. In the temple he acts with the authority of the Son in his Father's house, and his disciples remember Psalm 69:9: “Zeal for Your house will consume Me.” That psalm is the lament of a righteous sufferer, and consume hints at where Jesus' zeal will lead him. His answer to the demand for a sign points to the greatest sign, his resurrection. He is the new temple, the place where God meets his people, and after his body is destroyed and raised, worship will center on him rather than on a building in Jerusalem, a theme John develops in chapter 4.

hard.q: Did Jesus clear the temple at the beginning of his ministry, as John says, or at the end, as the other Gospels say?
hard.a: This is one of the clearest differences in order between John and the Synoptic Gospels. One view holds that there were two cleansings, which is possible since Jesus visited Jerusalem several times in John, and the details differ between the accounts. The other main view holds that there was one cleansing, and that one or more Gospel writers placed it where it best served their account. Ancient biographers often arranged material by theme rather than strict chronology, and John may have put the event at the start as a programmatic statement of Jesus' mission, much as Luke places the Nazareth sermon at the start of Jesus' ministry. Those who hold that John's order is chronological note that the forty-six years remark fits an early date. Christians who hold a high view of Scripture's truthfulness can be found on both sides, and the point of the event, Jesus' authority over the temple and his body as its fulfillment, is the same in all four Gospels.

questions: Jesus' first sign rescued a family from social embarrassment at a party. What does it tell you about him that he cared about such an ordinary need?
Mary told the servants, “Do whatever He tells you.” What is Jesus telling you to do that you have been reluctant to act on?
Jesus knew what was in every person and did not entrust himself to shallow faith. What distinguishes real faith from interest in what Jesus can do?
